  This paper takes this concept a step further by developing a combinatory logic 
  equivalent to the simply typed lambda calculus with recursion.
  The resulting system, called CRR, features a unique syntax where types are 
  indicated by the presence of corresponding self-application terms.
  The type inference method in CRR, or CRR inference, can be viewed as a 
  combination of the graph-based approach and a recursive type inference method.
  The paper shows that CRR inference matches the type safety and termination 
  properties of the recursive lambda calculus.
  Additionally, CRR provides a type-safe environment for translating the 
  recursive lambda calculus into combinatory logic without recursion.
  This translation serves as the basis for developing a recursive solver for 
  combinatory logic, or CRR solver.
  The CRR solver can be viewed as an efficient implementation of the graph-based 
  type inference method for the recursive lambda calculus.
  The paper also explores the relationship between CRR and existing type inference 
  methods for the lambda calculus with recursion. 
  Specifically, it compares CRR with the well-established method developed by 
  Hengcock and Mitchell, or H&M method.
  The key difference between these methods is that CRR uses a declarative 
  specification, whereas the H&M method employs an imperative approach.
  The paper outlines the challenges of extending CRR to typed lambda calculi with 
  higher types of recursion, or stronger type systems, or both.
  The CRR solver has been implemented in a Python-based environment and is 
  available for use by researchers and developers. 
  The paper's appendices include the formal definition of CRR, along with a 
  step-by-step example of using the CRR solver, and a side-by-side 
  comparison with the H&M method. 
  Furthermore, the paper includes a previously unpublished recursive solver for 
  the B\"ckner-Curry combinatory logic. 
  The paper also outlines an alternative implementation of the CRR solver that 
  utilizes a stack-based approach, along with a discussion on how this 
  implementation relates to the existing work by Clifton. 
  The paper further explores the connection between the CRR solver and the 
  recursive combinatory logic, or CRRL. 
  The paper also discusses how CRRL can be used to improve the efficiency 
  of the original CRR solver.

  the significance of understanding other agents, often referred to as "theory of mind"
  (ToM) or "cognitive empathy." This study investigates the potential benefits of ToM
  in AI through an innovative approach. We created a new game called "Empathy AI"
  that tests the capacity of AI to effectively collaborate with humans by incorporating
  ToM. In Empathy AI, two entities work together to manage multiple agents with
  conflicting interests, with one entity being human and the other being the AI system.
  We compared two AI models: a basic one that relies solely on data, and a more
  advanced ToM-capable model. Our results showed that the ToM-enabled model excelled
  in collaborative tasks, as measured by outcomes that considered factors like mutual
  benefit, loss prevention, and task completion. Furthermore, we discovered that
  this model successfully adopted the human perspective, as evidenced by its willingness
  to take on the human's risks and responsibilities. Our research discovered that
  training the ToM-enabled model to prioritize the human's point of view led to
  even better results. This approach has implications for developing more effective
  multi-agent systems that collaborate with humans, particularly in complex, dynamic
  environments. Our findings also underscore the significance of ToM in AI by showing
  its direct link to better cooperation and its capacity to reduce self-serving behavior. 
  This research is notable for highlighting the benefits of ToM in AI, specifically
  its capacity for genuine cooperation, as well as its potential to address critical
  issues like coordination, communication, and learning in multi-agent systems. 
  However, it's worth noting that creating ToM in AI is a highly challenging task that
  necessitates significant breakthroughs in fields like machine learning, robotics, and
  neuroscience.

The Asymptotic Sliding Lemma asserts that the visible part of the spine asymptotically approaches a translation invariant subset of the real line as the assemblage of disks shrinks towards its edge.  The lemma further implies that the underlying space of the assemblage can be represented as a sequence of disjoint intervals following the line of the real number.  In a recent paper, the first author established the Asymptotic Sliding Lemma for a specific type of assemblage of disks without a "gap" and demonstrated that it shares many characteristics with the model developed by Kenig and Reitz.  The current work extends the Asymptotic Sliding Lemma to all types of assemblage of disks and provides a detailed proof of its key properties.  The proof involves creating a new type of flow called the "sliding flow" and utilizing it to apply the Asymptotic Sliding Lemma to a specified type of assemblage of disks.  The work then delves into the more intricate "tight" configurations of the spine and ultimately establishes a connection between them and the "inner" edges of the underlying space of the assemblage.  The research presented in this paper was inspired by the ideas discussed in the recent paper of the first author, as well as the earlier work of Kenig and Reitz on the subject.  The paper aims to expand upon those concepts and provide a more comprehensive proof of the Asymptotic Sliding Lemma for all types of assemblage of disks.  The research relies on a combination of standard techniques from the field of Microlocal Analysis, as well as novel approaches to defining the "sliding flow" and the "visible part" of the spine.  The paper also explores the potential applications of the Asymptotic Sliding Lemma to studying the edge of the assemblage of disks and the underlying space of the assemblage through the use of the flow invariants.  The work on the Asymptotic Sliding Lemma is considered significant because it provides a rigorous proof of the lemma for all types of assemblage of disks and demonstrates the utility of the lemma in studying the edge of the assemblage of disks and the underlying space of the assemblage.  The research presented in this paper is believed to be of interest to a broad audience of mathematicians working on the subject of Microlocal Analysis and its various applications.

To counter this effect, developing efficient localization methods is crucial. This paper proposes a novel localization approach that leverages a dynamic optimization framework. It determines the optimal sampling rate, aiming to minimize the localization cost while keeping the error within an acceptable level. This was achieved through results obtained from realistic simulations, showing that the suggested method outperforms existing solutions by up to 25 times. Additionally, the optimization framework was tested on a real testbed, yielding results that generalized well to other unseen scenarios. The code for this research is openly available on GitHub. This paper presents a novel approach that achieves localization with a single anchor node. The algorithm starts by setting an initial wide coverage scanning rate. If not, the rate remains elevated to increase the detection range. The results show that the proposed algorithm excels over static solutions by up to 25 times. Previous approaches have relied on supervised learning, but we've developed an alternative method that leverages semantic role labeling without instruction. We trained a free aggregate detection model using a large corpus without removing context, then applied it to identify the combined entities and separate entities in a free aggregate context. Our findings show that this method successfully identifies free aggregates and combined entities, and our proposed evaluation metric captures the accuracy of this method in determining the relationships between entities. Additionally, we discovered that free aggregates can take the form of combined entities that are explicitly stated or implied, as well as separate entities that are explicitly stated or implied. We also observed that the relationships between entities can be identity, possession, location, path, association, attribution, communication, transportation, consumption, emission, entry, exit, state change, action, and inaction. Notably, our method's performance was evaluated using a small annotated dataset, but we believe there is a need for a more comprehensive and accurate set of annotations to better understand free aggregates. This research has implications for natural language processing, particularly in areas like information extraction, where combined entities and separate entities that are linked through relationships are extracted, and in areas like machine translation, where the translation of free aggregates is necessary to maintain the same level of coherence in the translated text as is present in the original text. To facilitate further research and development, we have created a set of annotated examples called Free Aggregate Data, which includes text with annotations showing the free aggregates, along with the corresponding semantic role labels, and we are making this resource publicly available. This is in contrast to other corpora that have been used for training and testing, which are often proprietary. We believe that making this corpus publicly available will help other researchers to further refine the free aggregate detection model and to train models using supervised learning. We also propose a new evaluation metric called the free aggregate detection F1 score, which is calculated by combining the recall and the precision of this method in identifying free aggregates, and we are making this metric publicly available to be used by other researchers. To address this limitation and better understand the connection between these variables, we used high-cadence optical and UV observations from the MAXI telescope on board the International Space Station for a comprehensive study of quiescent solar neutrino-producers. This dataset allowed us to track the optical and UV behavior of over 1000 events outside of solar flares and coronal mass ejections. The observed optical and UV spectra across the wavelength range from 0.1 to 2000 nm were analyzed to determine the energy, magnetic field strength, and total mass of ejecta in coronal mass ejections and to identify the physical processes governing the variability in the UV and optical regions. Our findings revealed that the energy and magnetic field strength in coronal mass ejections follow a power-law distribution with indices 1.5 and 2, respectively, and that the total mass of ejecta in coronal mass ejections is inversely related to the energy with an index of 1. The analysis also showed that the variability in the optical and UV regions exhibits distinct patterns and that the UV region is more sensitive to changes in the mass of coronal mass ejections. Furthermore, our study demonstrated that the first-order Rayleigh-Taylor instability dominates the evolution of coronal mass ejections and that these events can be modeled using a combination of magnetorotational instability, turbulence, and the Taylor-Sedov solution. Our research also enabled us to create a theoretical framework to predict the optical and UV output in the near-infrared and UV regions based on the energy and temperature of the neutron star, the mass and radius of the accretion disk, and the optical depth of the envelope. This framework was then used to calculate the optical and UV output for a subset of quiescent solar neutrino-producers and to compare our results with observations from the Hubble Space Telescope. Our findings further supported the hypothesis that the majority of solar neutrino-producers emit a small amount of energy in the form of electrons, antineutrinos, and neutrinos through the neutral current interaction. Our study also revealed that the optical and UV output of these quiescent solar neutrino-producers can be fit with a power-law distribution with an index 2.5 and that the most productive events can be detected by future neutrino detectors with energy sensitivities in the range from 10 to the power of 5 to 10 to the power of 9 erg. This framework enables the evaluation of torque acting on protoplanetary disks and influences the migration of exoplanets. Our goal is to investigate the consequences of applying this framework to observed data on exoplanary systems. Methods. We developed a theoretical model describing the hydrodynamic stability of protoplanetary disks in a simplified manner. This model includes the effects of various external forces on the orbital evolution of exoplanets. We then created a synthetic dataset of exoplanetary systems using Monte Carlo simulations based on this model. We explored different analysis techniques for this dataset, including linear regression and Bayesian inference. Results. We found that a linear relationship between certain parameters of exoplanetary systems does not always hold. However, we were able to establish a nonlinear relationship using Bayesian regression. This nonlinearity is primarily caused by the nonlinear effect of disk tidal ordering on the torque. Discussion. Our study highlights the importance of considering the nonlinearity when analyzing exoplanetary systems. We believe that incorporating hydrodynamic stability theory into the analysis provides a more accurate representation of the data. This nonlinearity can be observed in multiple dimensions and is crucial for a correct interpretation of the results. This approach can be further developed by accounting for uncertainties in the parameters of the model and the model itself, with possible extensions to more complex models of the hydrodynamic stability of protoplanetary disks. We establish two types of quantitative unique continuation results under different assumption sets. Firstly, assuming $u$ satisfies a second-order diffusion equation, we can recover the unique continuation result of Jerjen-Weiss and Rozenhstock with an improved polynomial factor. Secondly, we achieve a Carleman estimate on the hypersurface $M$ and apply it to a broad class of equations, including the Helmholtz equation and Klein-Gordon equations, both with and without external fields. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that unique continuation is possible with an exponentially decreasing weight, in contrast to the standard Carleman estimate, which requires a weight decreasing polynomially. Our proof involves microlocal techniques and decomposes solutions to equations as sums of decaying and growing components, where the growth rates are determined by the solution's initial data through the geometric scattering operator. This approach provides a framework for exploring the unique continuation of solutions with specific growth patterns.

Through a combination of magnetic field applications, cluster algorithms,

Our findings are compared with existing data and an asymptotic
analysis is also presented.
This research demonstrates a clear indication that strong
single-chain anisotropy is necessary for a classical spin $1/2$ Ising
chain to exhibit a first-order phase transition at a non-zero temperature. 
Contrary to expectations, we discovered that in some cases, the
curvature of the free energy can become negative in the low-temperature
phase, even for isolated chains, which has important implications
for the interpretation of experimental data, particularly those obtained
through specific heat measurements. 
Additionally, the effects of interchain coupling on this curvature
and the phase transition behavior is also examined. 
Our results also indicate that the end-point field strength
exponentiates with the single-chain anisotropy, an observation that
can be understood through a simplified two-field model. 
The effects of interchain coupling, the impact of boundary conditions,
and the behavior at the critical temperature were also numerically
computed. 
This research has implications for the interpretation of magnetic
measurements on molecular magnets. 
An analytical solution for the single-chain anisotropy is provided
in the appendix. 
This solution can serve as a reference for future numerical
method applications to magnetic molecules. 
An analysis of the curvature of the free energy at the phase transition
point is also presented. 
This analysis indicates that the negative curvature could be a
widespread phenomenon among exchange-coupled spins. 
Our results also indicate that the N\'{e}el temperature, which is a
critical parameter in the description of magnetic molecules, is not
necessarily a sharp threshold. 
Instead, it marks the beginning of a transition region. 
This fact has important implications for the interpretation of low
temperature specific heat measurements. 
Such measurements are crucial for the accurate description of
magnetic molecules. 
These results also indicate that the exchange-coupled spins exhibit
a first-order phase transition at temperatures that are several times
their N\'{e}el temperature.

  within the Standard Model and its extended versions. However, determining the
  type of spontaneous symmetry breaking, either electroweak or hadronic, is not
  straightforward due to its intricate relationship with non-perturbative QCD processes.
  This study uses a quark condensate as a measure of hadronic symmetry breaking
  and explores how it relates to the electroweak sector via the $\sigma$-meson, which
  acts as a mediator.
  A functional renormal group method is employed to examine the non-linear QCD
  dynamics and hadronic symmetry breaking in the flow of effective Lagrangians.
  Contrary to linear behavior in weak interactions, the hadronic sector exhibits
  non-linear characteristics when the quark condensate is affected by the
  electromagnetic and weak interactions.
  This study further investigates how hadronic symmetry breaking influences the
  electroweak sector, revealing a significant impact on the vacuum expectation value
  of the Higgs field, particularly in the case of the Standard Model and its
  extensions, such as the Standard Model Extended by a scalar field that couples
  strongly to the quark condensate. 
  Calculations are performed to determine the mass ranges of certain scalar
  resonances that emerge at TeV energies, which could be within the reach of
  upcoming particle colliders. 
  The research also highlights the crucial role that upcoming experiments, such
  as the ELN and the Future Circular Hadron Collider, will play in confirming
  the nature of hadronic symmetry breaking through direct scalar production
  and decay.

  Z'\rightarrow e^+e^- \tau^+\tau^-$ process at the International Linear
  Collider is also presented as a concrete example of how to achieve an
  order of magnitude improvement in detecting a 5 TeV scalar resonance.

  combination of radiative rejection techniques in the calorimeter system,
  as illustrated in Figure 5, along with other optimisation strategies

By using Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations at non-zero temperatures, we generated extensive datasets for two to five disorder parameters. These datasets allowed us to perform multiple reweighting steps to the strong coupling limit, effectively bridging the gap between small and large coupling strengths. Our study confirms previous findings that the thermal transition in this complex theory exhibits first-order behavior at small couplings and gradually transitions to a second-order behavior as the coupling strengthens. Notably, we were able to accurately capture the disorder parameter in the strong coupling limit, which was previously estimated as between 2.5 to 3.5. Our results indicate that this value lies within the narrow range of 2.8 to 3.0. Additionally, we reweighted the transition diagrams themselves, which also indicated a shift from convex to concave shapes as the coupling increased. Our research further explores the connection to the strong coupling limit by utilizing the loop expansion method. This approach involves integrating out low-energy modes to obtain a effective $\phi^4$ theory. Our analysis reveals that the effective coupling in this context is indeed closer to unity, which aligns with our reweighted disorder parameters. This effective theory is effectively a mean-field approximation, which can be solved exactly. Our exact solutions include both the thermal transition in the complex $\phi^4$ theory as well as the thermal transition in the real $\phi^4$ theory. Notably, the reweighted disorder parameter in the real $\phi^4$ theory is found to be 2.62, which can be compared to other existing estimates. Our research also involved a critical examination of various reweighting procedures. We found that our results from reweighting three disorder parameters already yield accurate predictions. This suggests that reweighting only a single parameter, which is the free energy, may be sufficient to obtain reliable predictions for the strong coupling limit. Our research implies that the reweighting procedure can be efficiently applied to other thermal field theories. This involves conducting initial simulations at small couplings and then using reweighting to access the strong coupling limit. This approach can help avoid the significant computational costs associated with direct simulations at large couplings. Our results also underscore the limitations of reweighting to the strong coupling limit by highlighting the importance of reweighting multiple disorder parameters when the initial simulations were conducted at a finite coupling strength. This is because the effective disorder parameters at large couplings can differ from their small coupling

by its ability to resist 
  malicious node attacks and withstand system failures. To achieve this, most 
  blockchain networks utilize a consensus algorithm that requires participating nodes 
  to agree on a common block, with algorithms like PBFT and Raft being widely 
  adopted. In contrast, stateless blockchain networks permit the creation and 
  dissemination of blocks without a centralized consensus mechanism. These networks 
  generate blocks based on state that has already been established, with the 
  block's validity determined by the network's users whose associated nodes have 
  access to the underlying state. If a node attempts to transmit an invalid block 
  to another node, it will be rejected, with the creator of the block subject to 
  financial penalties. As a result, malicious nodes face significant losses if 
  they attempt to spread blocks outside of the network's legitimate state, giving 
  these networks inherent fault tolerance properties that can be formally verified 
  and validated through actual implementation testing. This paper introduces the 
  concept of stateless blockchain networks, outlines their technical components, 
  and compares them to traditional blockchain networks. It also presents the formal 
  specification and verification of a simple stateless blockchain protocol, 
  along with the testing and validation of a more complex protocol implementation 
  in a real-world scenario. Overall, the paper and associated code provide a 
  starting point for further research, development, and testing of these 
  resilient blockchain networks. The developer tested the protocol on a scale of 
  100 nodes and made the entire code available on GitHub. The code includes 
  protocols for simple and complex stateless blockchain networks, along with

future 100 TeV hadron colliders, the identification of large transverse momentum jets will need to be highly efficient, accurate, and robust in the presence of significant multijet backgrounds. To this end, the use of jet substructure techniques is being highly considered. This research develops advanced algorithms for detecting highly vibrating quark condensates, also known as heavy quarks, within the jets produced at these high-energy levels. A novel approach is presented to predict the substructure of jets by utilizing neural network simulations, which are then compared to existing models based on probabilistic distributions and parton showers. It is demonstrated that neural network-driven predictions can accurately replicate underlying truth with high precision, surpassing traditional models' performance. Furthermore, a new issue emerges in the form of heavy quark subjet discrimination, characterized by a conflict between raising the energy threshold for improved prediction accuracy and the need to account for high-energy subjets. A series of strategies is explored to address this problem by integrating additional network components, multiplying output values by density functions, and directly predicting subjet multiplicities. These developments are put into practice by training and evaluating neural network models on various datasets, including those representing the substructure of heavy quark jets at 100 TeV colliders. The results show that neural networks achieve high precision when predicting various jet characteristics, including the energy of the subjet that first exceeds a certain transverse momentum threshold, the multiplicity of subjets exceeding a given transverse momentum threshold, and the distance in pseudorapidity of the first subjet exceeding a certain transverse momentum threshold. The introduction of additional variables, such as jet and subjet pseudorapidities, as well as the inclusion of minimal substructure information, are found to enhance the precision of heavy quark substructure prediction. The code for this research is made publicly available, and the approach is found to be scalable and suitable for real-time applications at future hadron colliders. The training and evaluation of heavy quark substructure neural networks on larger datasets, representing multiple interactions and more advanced jet substructure, are also discussed as potential areas for further development. This research thesis is accompanied by an extensive dataset of 1 million records, each containing the details of a jet with a heavy quark substructure, and is available for public use. This dataset is a crucial step towards creating more complex jet substructure simulations that can be utilized by researchers and physicists for the development of efficient heavy quark substructure identification algorithms for future hadron colliders. A finite monomial extension of a group G is defined as the image of G under a monomial embedding, where a monomial embedding is defined as a composition of Baer embeddings and twisted embeddings. A Baer embedding of a group H into a group K is defined as an embedding that fixes the center of H within the center of K.  A twisted embedding of a group H into a group K is an embedding such that some power of the twisted embedding corresponds to a Baer embedding.  The universal covering group of a finite group G is defined as the group whose elements in relation to G are the same as the cosets of the commutator subgroup of G within its free product over the left cosets of G by its commutator subgroup.  A free product of a group A by the left cosets of B, where B is the commutator subgroup of A, is defined as the group whose defining relations are the defining relations of A and the relations derived from the interaction between the elements of A and the left cosets of B.  The commutator subgroup of a group A is defined as the subgroup generated by the commutators of A, which are products of an element and its inverse written in a specific order.  A free product of a family of groups A indexed by a set I is defined as the group whose defining relations are the defining relations of the groups A and the relations derived from the interaction between the elements of the groups A and the indices in the set I.   of quaternionic and octonionic algebras as anti-commutative generated algebras.

  In particular, it delves into the specifics of the quaternionic Heisenberg 
  uncertainty principle and the octonionic version of the Yang-Baxter equation. 
  It also touches on the subject of defining the index of a quaternionic line 
  bundle over a quaternionic curve. 
  In the process, we draw comparisons between the approaches to these problems 
  and those employable within the framework of arithmetic geometry.

  criteria.

  and simple machine learning models. 
  The remaining set of actions is then passed on to the Continuous Memory MCTS 
  algorithm for further evaluation.

  room for improvement.

  as the search progresses, as well as a strategy to utilize a separate, smaller

We develop a mathematical framework to examine the competitive dynamics of two population types with overlapping distribution spaces, incorporating both intrinsic preferences and external obstacles. Our approach results in a system of partial differential equations (PDEs) that models the spatial and temporal interactions between these populations. Through a linear stability analysis of the monomorphic model, we find that the intrinsic preference of a population can lead to skewed distributions, while the effect of spatial obstacles depends on their size and results in populations adapting to fill the available space in a manner analogous to a specific probability distribution. We also extend the analysis to include immigant cells in the monomorphic model and a linearized version of the polymorphic model, and apply these findings to understand the competitive dynamics between different population types. Our numerical simulations confirm our analytical predictions and explore various spatial scenarios, revealing that the competitive dynamics can give rise to bistable states, leading to the exclusion of one population type from certain areas of the distribution space. Our study provides a foundation for further investigation into the temporal changes within these systems, using tools such as the Alfven-Hermite method or the finite element method. I) is a seismic imaging technique that has the
  potential to overcome the limitations of traditional Hybrid Imaging methods.
  Hybrid Imaging methods combine the advantages of both Differential
  Interpolation and Remigration techniques to mitigate the discontinuity issue
  caused by migration operators that don't honor the Laplacian property.
  However, Hybrid Imaging methods require a highly accurate initial model, 
  which is often difficult to achieve in practice.
  On the other hand, FWI has the capability to produce a model that honors the
  correct physics, as it minimizes the misfit between the recorded seismic data
  and the simulated data obtained through remigration.
  Despite its benefits, the convergence of FWI is impeded by local minima and
  the large nonlinearity of the problem.
  To address these challenges, a new Hybrid FWI method has been developed by
  integrating the advantages of Hybrid Imaging with the power of FWI.
  This new method, which is referred to as Hybrid FWI, involves the use of
  the residual from the current iteration as the source wavefield in the
  simulation step of FWI.
  By doing so, the method ensures that the wavefield honors the Laplacian
  property, thus preventing the creation of artificial discontinuities and
  ensuring a smooth and continuous model.
  The hybrid version of the algorithm was tested on a 3D synthetic example
  with real earth properties and 20km of source-receiver spacing.
  The results showed that the algorithm was able to recover a model with a
  resolution of 15m in a single run with 13 iterations.
  The feasibility of implementing this algorithm on a 3D real-data set was
  also demonstrated by applying it to a record section from the EAGE 2011
  challenge data set.
  The results showed that the algorithm was able to recover a model with a
  resolution of 20m in a single run with 10 iterations.
  The code for the new Hybrid FWI method has been made available for public
  use on GitHub at the address https://github.com/ahmadijouy/ahmadi_jouy_2022_cse.
  The code requires the use of the open-source software Pysigpy for data
  simulation and the Matrelos library for optimization.

involves identifying the minimum amount of malicious input required to confidently deceive a given machine learning model into producing an erroneous prediction. This adverse input is known as the worst-case attack budget. To determine this worst-case attack budget, we need a computational model that can optimize both the amount of malicious input and model misclassification. However, as machine learning models are typically based on neural networks, their lack of efficient differentiable mechanisms makes them incompatible with optimized malicious input generation. To address this incompatibility, we propose a new computational model that uses a neural network-based classifier in conjunction with a neural network-based attacker, resulting in an efficient and scalable way to find the worst-case attack budget. The efficacy of this model is demonstrated through successful optimization of both the adverse input and model misclassification across multiple neural network-based classifiers, highlighting the broad applicability of this model. The results show that the proposed model significantly reduces the computational cost required to find the worst-case attack budget by up to three orders of magnitude in comparison with alternative computational methods. This efficiency enables the model to handle complex real-world neural network-based classifiers that are otherwise intractable. The code for the proposed model is available at https://github.com/yinghaoxi/WCAB.   of the disability. This information can be used to adjust the assessment's level
  of difficulty. An evaluation of the system's performance using a weighted score

  difficulty (r = 0.87). This indicated that the system can effectively adjust
  assessment difficulty in response to a child's abilities. An interview with a
  specialist in physical education also found that the system's assessments were
  consistent with their own evaluations. This research and the developed framework

  assessments that can automatically adjust difficulty levels based on the abilities

  a crucial step in various semantic parsing tasks. The model, a deep neural 
  network based on a convolutional neural network, processes words and their 
  dependencies individually before integrating all information to determine 
  chunk labels. We achieve this individualized analysis through a novel 
  'gated' mechanism, where each word's output is determined by a weighted 
  combination of a basic representation and a complex, dependency-based 
  representation. We further develop a unique way to handle character n-grams 
  and integrate this unique feature into a general framework. The model's 
  performance is evaluated on the RTE PARC subtask; with minimal pretraining, 
  it surpasses existing results on the same dataset. 

  We also introduce a new public dataset, called ChunksGo, which addresses 
  a significant limitation in the field by providing chunked labels for a 
  large, open-domain dialogue. The dataset's evaluation reveals several 
  interesting findings, such as the challenge of distinguishing between 
  attributive and appositive prepositional phrases. The ChunksGo dataset, 
  along with the proposed model, also serve as a starting point for 
  developing other semantic parsing applications. The model and dataset are 
  publicly available on GitHub and Hugging Face Hub.

  (1) The model secures a 3.3 F-score improvement on the test set of the 
  small RTE PARC subtask and a 2.5 F-score improvement on the validation 
  set of the larger RTE PARC full task through 5-fold cross-validation. 
  (2) The ChunksGo dataset yields a new state-of-the-art F-score of 92.1 
  on the test set of the small RTE PARC subtask.

  various domains and tasks by serving as a solid base for further 
  development in other semantic parsing applications. 
  (4) The model and ChunksGo show that pretraining is not always 
  necessary, as the model performs well with minimal training. 
  (5) The model and ChunksGo highlight the significance of individual 
  word analysis in phrase chunking. 
  (6) The model and ChunksGo emphasize the importance of distinguishing 
  between attributive and appositive prepositional phrases.

This paper presents a quantum control system called "Quantum Router" that enables a highly quantum-capable control system by minimizing the quantum depth of its own gate sequence.  This is achieved through a new gate sequence generation algorithm based on the "Braslet-Lossy" method.  Research shows that the Quantum Router outperforms existing control systems, such as qdrift, on a wide range of applications, including the simulation of quantum spin systems, certain types of error correction codes, and specific cryptographic protocols.  The Quantum Router has the added benefit of maintaining small quantum depth, making it highly suitable for scaling to larger, more complex quantum processors. Our work builds on the concept of the group measure space framework and generalizes the ideas of Durham and the second author for groups to the discrete time setting, establishing relationships with the graded versions of the Poisson processes and proving that these processes lead to the G-Brownian motion process when combined with a natural translation invariant measure on G. We introduce the graded version of the Poisson-Bernoulli process on a group G below, and its discrete time incarnation is defined as an extension of the Bernoulli field that assigns to each subgroup of G a measure on the coset space G/K, in a way that is invariant to the choice of the subgroup. This process can be further characterized as the collection of measures obtained by applying the conditional measure operator to the standard Bernoulli process on the power set of G, with the condition defined by the invariant sigma-algebra generated by the coset relations.

  domain. We demonstrate the effectiveness of offense transfer through a study on 
  three distinct permissive domains (Twitter, Yelp, and Amazon reviews) and a 
  regulated domain (finance), using a limited set of labeled data from the 
  regulated domain and a large set of labeled data from the permissive domains.

  baseline transfer and training from scratch in the regulated domain.

  overlap with the regulated domain does not always produce the best results, 
  indicating that offense transfer can adapt from diverse permissive domains.

By conducting a combined experimental and numerical analysis of a copper cylinder dissolving in air, this study categorizes the cylinder's dissolution regime into three main areas: the leached core, the transition zone, and the outer layer.  A newly developed parameter, the superimposed Peclet number, is found to dictate the transfer regime when natural convection is present.  As a result, four transfer regimes are identified: the control regime, where convection is driven by the outer layer; the limited transfer regime, where the outer layer restricts mass transfer from the core; the assisted regime, where the outer layer speeds up mass transfer from the core; and the isolated regimes, where the core and outer layer transfer independently.  As natural convection strengthens, the assisted regime emerges as the most common transfer regime.  This research offers a comprehensive understanding of the factors influencing mass transfer from composite cylinders and highlights the importance of distinguishing the leached core, the transition zone, and the outer layer in calculating the total mass transfer.  As such, this study proposes combining the leached core and the transition zone as the effective cylinder diameter.  Furthermore, it shows that the length of the transition zone is minimal when natural convection is present but becomes more significant as convection weakens.  As a consequence, the effective cylinder diameter may increase under conditions with little convection, leading to a broader range of cylinder diameters that fall under the limited transfer regime than previously thought.  This study's results also indicate that the thickness of the outer layer does not affect the transfer regime to the same extent as the diameter of the core.  As a result, this study's numerical data can be applied more broadly, such as to cylinders with different materials and geometries, without the need for additional parameters. To this end, we identify two rare decay modes that could indicate lepton-flavour non-universality in $B^0_s \rightarrow \mu\mu$ events: $B^0_s \rightarrow \phi\mu\mu$ and $B^0_s \rightarrow K^*\mu\mu$. By utilizing LHCb data from 2010 to 2019, we constrain the rates for these two decay modes. Based on these constraints and current non-universality limits, we use a Monte Carlo simulation to investigate the prospects for discovering lepton-flavour non-universality in $B^0_s \rightarrow \mu\mu$ events at the LHCb experiment in the near future. Our findings suggest that with an integrated luminosity of 300 inverse picobarns at the LHC, the LHCb experiment could determine whether $B^0_s \rightarrow \phi\mu\mu$ and $B^0_s \rightarrow K^*\mu\mu$ processes exhibit non-universality in the muon sector, with rates equivalent to 5% deviating from the standard model predictions in 95% confidence intervals. Alternatively, with an integrated luminosity of 300 inverse picobarns, the LHCb experiment could determine whether $B^0_s \rightarrow \phi\mu\mu$ and $B^0_s \rightarrow K^*\mu\mu$ processes exhibit non-universality in the muon sector, with rates equivalent to 10% deviating from the standard model predictions in 84% confidence intervals.

Our system has a quantum critical point at finite interaction strength, characterized by a linear temperature dependence of the resistivity and a specific heat coefficient. A comparison with experimental results from Sr$_{x}$Cu$_{8-x}($Si$_{0.5}-$Ga$_{0.5})$$_{6}$ shows a degree of similarity with a quantum critical point in a 2D Hubbard model on a square lattice, despite the different dimensionality. An examination of the real and orbital spaces reveals that the quantum critical point occurs at a larger interaction strength when considering the total density of states. An analysis of the real-space orbital occupancies reveals an exponential decay with increasing distance from the central atom, indicating that the quantum critical point behaves as a one-dimensional Fermi liquid. An examination of the orbital occupancies in the high-energy bands shows that they remain unchanged with respect to filling, indicating that the quantum critical point is driven by the filling imbalance between the two bands rather than the band itself. An investigation of the effective mass enhancement as a function of temperature shows a saturation at high temperatures, indicating that the quantum critical point can be described as a one-dimensional Fermi liquid at finite temperature. An examination of the orbital occupancies in the high-energy bands as a function of the number of holes shows a linear decrease with a slope that corresponds to the charge gap in a half-filled lattice, indicating that the quantum critical point behaves as a one-dimensional BCS-like superconductor in the limit of small hole doping. An investigation of the finite-temperature phase diagram reveals a transition from the quantum critical point to a mean-field BCS-like superconductor at a finite energy scale, which can be influenced by both the hole doping and the energy cutoff. An examination of the real and orbital spaces reveals that the dominant contribution to the specific heat comes from the central atoms, indicating that the quantum critical point behaves as an orbital and one-dimensional Fermi/BCS-like superconductor.   involves a significant distinction between cooperative and competitive tasks.
  For example, in a collaborative robotics environment, agents may work together
  to transport heavy loads but individually strive to reach high speeds.
  Due to this dual nature, traditional MARL methods are no longer fully 
  effective, leading to the emergence of a new field that studies both 
  collaborative and competitive scenarios.
  This paper presents a novel framework known as Competitive-Cooperative Multi-
  Agent Reinforcement Learning (CCMARL), which organizes existing methods 
  within this field and provides a theoretical foundation for future research.
  CCMARL is divided into four key categories: (1) learning collaborative 
  policies, (2) determining competitive aspects, (3) balancing cooperative and 
  competitive behaviors, and (4) addressing stability and convergence issues.
  By offering a comprehensive overview and categorization of CCMARL, 
  along with a hypothetical example, this framework aims to facilitate 
  research, development, and knowledge sharing within the community. 
  Specifically, the framework's benefits are illustrated through a simple 
  simulation, which demonstrates how modifying a single model parameter 
  across different CCMARL categories can lead to contrasting outcomes. 
  This framework and the associated insights are expected to guide researchers 
  and practitioners in creating innovative, competitive-cooperative MARL models.

Specifically, we establish convergence norms of order $\sqrt{\log(n)}$ for these sums or sequences, which can be viewed as strengthened versions of the Weak Law of Large Numbers. If the time-varying distribution functions are held fixed, these convergence norms reduce to $\sqrt{\log(n)}$, as expected. The results are accompanied by upper and lower bounds examples, demonstrating the tightness of these norms in various scenarios. The proof of these convergence norms relies on an inequality that can be viewed as an enhanced version of the Bernstein inequality, with an upper norm of order $\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\log(n)}$ among the most precise known estimates for this kind of inequalities. The examples are based on a newly defined concept, the subgaussian type of a random variable, which can be useful in other contexts as well. The proof of the convergence norms also involves a newly introduced method of controlling the maximum of a set of i.i.d. subgaussian random variables, which can be viewed as a strengthened version of the Borell-Sudarev inequality. The results and the associated inequalities can be viewed as an extension of the weak law of large numbers from constant distributions to time-varying distributions. The main ideas and the related technical results presented here are applicable in their own right in various subgaussian-type scenarios. However, these apps have significant limitations in identifying individuals who may inadvertently spread the virus when experiencing symptoms, as they rely solely on user reports for notification purposes. To address this challenge, we present a novel algorithm that leverages data from these contact tracing apps to detect potential virus transmission hotspots by analyzing the spread of the virus. The proposed method utilizes a compartmental model to create a mathematical framework representing the spread of the virus, before developing a discrete-time dynamic model to evaluate the change in infected individual counts over time. The algorithm determines the transmission risk of each contact by combining the virus's incubation period, the apps' detection delay, and the model's parameters. It then calculates the potential impact of each contact on the virus's transmission, taking into account the probability of symptoms appearing in the source individual, the probability of detection through app input, and the parameters of the model. The algorithm ranks contacts in order of transmission risk and utilizes a first-order autoregressive model to identify the time frame when the app would have detected the contact if the source individual had reported it, if the source individual's symptoms appeared immediately. It further estimates the number of new infections generated by each contact, utilizing a linear interpolation to calculate the change in infected individual counts over the time frame when the source individual's symptoms appeared. The algorithm determines the fraction of these new infections that were reported through the app, accounting for the detection rate, the probability of the source individual reporting the contact, and the probability of the app detecting the contact. It then calculates the weighted sum of the potential impact of each contact, using the fraction of reported new infections as the weight. The algorithm ranks the contacts in order of transmission risk and identifies the top contacts as the potential virus transmission hotspots. It marks these contacts as high-risk and incorporates this information into the discrete-time dynamic model to forecast the change in infected individual counts over the next time period. The algorithm repeats this process for each time period to forecast the future spread of the virus. It evaluates the proposed algorithm on a realistic simulation of the initial spread of the virus in Wuhan, the epicenter of the COVID-19 pandemic, and on a simulation of the measles outbreak in a small world network. It demonstrates that the algorithm detects the transmission risk of high-risk contacts and the virus transmission hotspots accurately, and that it can handle a large number of contacts and a long incubation period without losing efficiency.   research based on German measles data and reveals that all variables influence

  effect. This study's results provide a reliable estimation method for the R

  emerge as universally applicable across different contexts. This research is an

To realize its potential, it's essential to understand the interplay between spin and electronic properties through accurate measurements of magnetic relaxation and optical polarization decay. To this end, we use pump-probe spectroscopy in a time and phase-resolved manner to investigate the optical polarization lifetime and decay patterns in both the linear and nonlinear responses of An2. Ariel's massive antenna allows it to transmit extensive data via a technique called phase modulation, a method whose effectiveness depends on its being unaffected by the solar wind. The solar wind, a stream of charged particles emanating from the sun, could potentially impact Ariel's measurements by introducing an artificial opacity that interferes with its own signals, very similar in scale to its own antenna. To assess this threat, researchers simulated transmission processes that mimic the solar wind's interaction with the antenna, modeled as a perfectly conducting sphere, using full-wave electromagnetic numerical methods, specifically the finite element method. They examined various solar wind conditions by modifying the plasma density and temperature, and investigated the effects on the antenna's transmission by measuring its scattering cross-section, specifically its imaginary component, which indicates opacity. The results of these simulations match the predictions of a simplified model called the "effective permittivity approximation" and demonstrate that the antenna's opacity is minimal when the solar wind's impact is viewed from its own direction. Consequently, the influence of the solar wind on Ariel's measurements is expected to be negligible. Nonetheless, this analysis serves as a starting point for addressing potential sources of opacity in the Ariel mission, and similar phenomena may be relevant for other deep space research missions that transmit large amounts of data via powerful antennas.   tasks: one for individual steps and another for validating the existence of

  introduces the Bounded Timed Reachability Problem, which involves determining
  if there exists a step that results in a timing relationship leading to a

  in polynomial time, which was previously unknown. Additionally, this research
  introduces the forward reachability analysis for the BCECA model and shows it
  can be performed in a polynomial time, which is a significant result in itself
  as well as a component of the Bounded Timed Reachability Problem solution.  A

  class, which includes properties that can be verified for any step within a
  certain time frame from a given state. The main contribution of this research
  is demonstrating that both BCECA and event-clock automata with a decidable
  future time property can perform forward reachability analysis in a polynomial
  time, which in turn enables the solution of the Bounded Timed Reachability

The model in question uses a fully nonlinear, 1D version of the Klein-Gordon equation to analyze the ion's dynamics while disregarding any higher spatial and temporal fluctuations of the laser field. Nonlinear interactions between the ions and the laser field lead to the creation of unusual, cavity-filled electron holes, also known as "vacuum holes," at the edge of the ion cloud. methods and programming languages on beginning programmers' understanding of recursion 
and their general programming abilities. Twenty first-semester education students 
participated in the study, learning a basic programming course with one of three 
curricula for a month. Each curriculum used a different approach: an imperative 
language, a functional language, or a combination of both languages. The students' 
progress was evaluated through tests on recursion and programming concepts, as 
well as their completion of tasks to find recursive solutions in various scenarios.

results in understanding recursion and developing their general programming skills. 
However, it is essential to note that the study had a limited sample size and was 
carried out under controlled conditions, similar to a laboratory setting, which 
may not reflect real-world teaching situations. Further research is necessary to 
confirm these findings in various educational environments.

  this difficulty by developing an approach to detect and identify co-planted
  documents that span multiple languages without access to labeled data. The
  proposed technique leverages structural and semantic properties of text to
  detect plagiarism across languages, and it is evaluated using synthetic data. 
  The assessment shows that document detection based on monolingual features is
  less effective than the proposed multi-language approach, and the technique
  generalizes well to different document structures. Additionally, it is found
  that detecting co-planted documents in the same dataset does not provide
  meaningful results, indicating that each document was independently planted,
  and the technique is effective at identifying documents with similar content
  across different languages, even if there is no overlap. 
  The assessment method has limitations because it is based solely on detection
  rather than on the characteristics of security threats in the particular domain
  it is tested on, which consists of public announcements. 
  The results demonstrate that while the technique works on the provided dataset
  of security threats, it may not generalize to other domains due to the diverse
  nature of public announcements. 
  The assessment also highlights the current shortcomings of threat detection
  systems on the web, specifically that they can be easily compromised by
  posting meaningless text as security threats. 
  The research on the assessment of the technique is valuable for understanding
  the challenges in evaluating security threat detection systems. 
  The assessment indicates that more nuanced methods are needed to evaluate
  detection systems, such as analyzing search queries and the structure of
  announcements, and to consider the diverse nature of public announcements. 
  The assessment of the technique is further validated through a survey with
  experts in the field of security and computer science. 
  The experts were able to distinguish 30\% of the security threats from 70\% of
  random public announcements. 
  The assessment also shows that the distinguishing features of security threats
  include words related to security, official domains, and quotes from officials
  which are often used to give the announcements credibility. 
  The assessment of the technique is also compared to a machine learning-based
  approach on a new set of public announcements. 
  The comparison shows that the proposed technique is more effective than the
  machine learning-based approach in identifying security threats.

By analyzing the scaling of this parameter with time, our research examines the trade-off between the desire for innovation and the constraints of resource management. Modern  networks  are too complex to function in a way that individual neurons can,  thus raising questions about their fundamental behavior. This study  investigates the internal processes of neural networks in relation  to their predictive capabilities by examining how local patterns within  the data can be represented and generalized. We observe that neural  networks effectively represent unusual data points as outliers,  which they treat differently than typical data. This distinction  is found to be critical in forecasting, as it allows the network  to avoid making similar mistakes in the future. Through a series  of experiments and theoretical analysis, we show that the  effectiveness of this approach is not limited to the data used  in training and demonstrates an improvement in forecasting  performance when compared to other methods widely used in the field.  This difference in network behavior is quantified by an index  that reflects the degree to which a network classifies data  points as typical or unusual, which in turn affects how it  forecasts those same points. This index is further examined  in relation to forecasting performance over time and is found  to be a key factor in reducing the persistence with which unusual  data points are forecasted. This research is illustrated through  a real-world forecasting scenario involving economic instability  at the local level. This study provides a starting point  for further research on the intricacies of neural networks,  which is essential given the widespread and expanding  applications of this technology in forecasting and beyond.   Our results reveal that, contrary to the observed phenomenon, a calculation
  without considering the effects of long-range Coulomb interactions shows a
  hardening in the dispersion of the Ti-related phonon modes. On the other hand,
  when we include the effects of long-range Coulomb interactions, we obtain a
  scenario that closely resembles the experimental results. Here we propose that
  the enhanced electron-phonon interaction in Nb-doped SrTi3d is, in fact, a
  manifestation of the marginal instability of this material towards a Kohn
  shockwave state, which is a new concept we introduce in this study. A Kohn
  shockwave state refers to a situation where a long-wavelength phonon mode
  exhibits positive dispersion in a three-dimensional lattice. Our findings also
  suggest that doping SrTi3d will result in a shift towards a long-wavelength
  phonon mode that has zero energy at a finite wavevector, which would be a
  prediction testable by inelastic X-ray scattering experiments.  We further
  emphasize that the phrase 'Kohn shockwave' specifically alludes to a
  long-wavelength phonon mode that exhibits positive dispersion in a three
  dimensional lattice, which is a direct consequence of long-range Coulomb
  interactions, as demonstrated by the calculations. However, we also note that
  in a two-dimensional lattice, a long-wavelength phonon mode that has zero
  energy at a finite wavevector can arise without the influence of long-range
  Coulomb interactions, as shown by the calculations. In such a scenario, we
  would not describe it as a Kohn shockwave. Thus, we propose that the term
  'Kohn shockwave' should be used to describe a long-wavelength phonon mode
  that exhibits positive dispersion in a three-dimensional lattice, which can
  arise as a result of long-range Coulomb interactions, as a consequence of

  Nibe et al reporting a transition at 4.7 K in a nickelate thin film on

  To investigate the spatial variation of this transition, researchers used
  synchrotron radiation to examine the spatial distribution of Nibe et al's
  nickelate thin film.
  By comparing the distribution of lattice parameters with the distribution
  of the metal-insulator phase transition temperature, researchers found
  that the transition temperature decreases with an increase in the rate
  of dislocation defects in the nickelate thin film.
  This can be explained by the dislocations acting as a type of linear
  defect that obstructs the nickelate's lattice symmetry, thus affecting
  the electron filling and local curvature of the lattice in the nickelate
  and causing a decrease in Tc.
  This effect becomes more pronounced at higher Tc values and is linked
  to the disorder that occurs in the nickelate's electron filling near
  its disorder-driven metal-insulator phase transition.
  As a result, the lattice disorder caused by the lago and ruto substrates
  accelerates this disorder-driven metal-insulator phase transition in
  the nickelate, leading to the 4.7 K Tc value observed by Nibe et al.
  This acceleration can be seen in the film's middle section, which
  has the highest lattice disorder and Tc value, while the film's edges
  have less lattice disorder and Tc values.  This acceleration manifests

  and can be described by an equation that includes a linear term
  that describes this spatial variation, and has been used to predict
  Tc values in other nickelate thin films with varying levels of
  disorder, such as point and planar defects.
  This prediction was verified by inserting a step or a trench in some
  of the nickelate thin films, which resulted in an increase in the
  disorder and a corresponding increase in the Tc values in those areas. A dominating set with the minimum number of vertices is referred to as a $\gamma$-set or a dominating set of size $\gamma$ for that particular graph. The concept of a dominating set can be modified to accommodate time-varying graphs, with a time-dominating set defined as a set of vertices such that for every vertex in the graph's vertex set, there exists a point in time when the vertex is adjacent to at least one vertex within the time-dominating set. The time required for this condition to be met for each vertex can vary, and it must be recorded as a time is written in parentheses at the end of the entry. For example, the time-dominating set $\{v_1,(v_2,3)\},$ indicates that the time it takes for $v_2$ to be adjacent to $v_1$ is 3 time units. The time it takes for a time-dominating set to dominate the time-varying graph can be represented as the maximum time it takes for a vertex not in the time-dominating set to be adjacent to a vertex in the time-dominating set. The time-dominating number of a time-varying graph is then defined as the minimum size of a time-dominating set that can dominate the graph within the maximum time. This research focuses on time-dominating sets and time-dominating numbers of line graphs, with specific examples and general properties established. Additionally, several new concepts, the time-$\gamma$-number, time-$\kappa$-number, and the time that takes to reach a clique, are also introduced and their calculation illustrated with time-varying line graphs. This result supplements our initial result, as it implies that the Boolean function complexity of a half-space in the $n$-dimensional Boolean hypercube cannot be calculated using $n$ bits, leading to an upper bound on the efficiency of algorithms for this problem. This study addresses this gap by developing an all-NVIDIA Cup acceleration framework for a high-performance dense linear solver, specifically designed for the NVIDIA Cup architecture.   2.02 times at a scale of 10 GeV.

  falloff of parton densities with increasing scale mirrors their impact on the base
  parton densities, albeit with a more pronounced effect.

  equations results in an improved match between theoretical cross sections and those
  measured in experiments, with a relative improvement of 3.5\% on average.

  utilized in place of standard DGLAP equations for further precise theoretical
  predictions.  We also introduce a new variable, the quark density at a scale of a

  offering a potential proxy for describing light-quark distributions within hadrons.

  incorporating the influence of coherent electromagnetic interactions on parton evolution.

This phenomenon was first observed by Ludwig Stark in 1969 during an experiment and later studied mathematically by Carol Wilson in 1981. In this paper, a new approach is taken to study the Stokes phenomenon, by applying the multisummation method to express a solution as a series of positive terms rather than using power series. This approach provides more details about the solution's behavior in the interval where the Stokes phenomenon occurs. Specifically, the length of the interval where the phenomenon appears as a sharp edge rather than a point can be determined. This method was successfully applied to study the Stokes phenomenon in a differential equation whose coefficients vary smoothly with a complex variable, a rotationally symmetric harmonic polynomial, and the Bessel differential equation. These studies involved determining the location and length of the interval where the phenomenon occurs, which can be used to interpret the results of the experiment that first observed the phenomenon.   but at a cost of substantial computational requirements. To address this
  limitation, this study introduces a simplified attention mechanism
  called ``Structured Attention'' that reduces attention calculation
  between sequences by arranging data sequences into a two-dimensional
  grid and calculating attention within this grid. This mechanism is
  particularly effective for tasks involving long sequences. In addition,
  to further minimize computational costs, a new multi-head scaled
  dot-product query-key value mechanism is proposed that maintains
  performance while reducing memory and processing requirements.
  These innovations are integrated into a lightweight Transformer-based
  model called ``FastTransformer'' that outperforms standard
  Transformer models in several tasks, including machine translation,
  summarization, and part-of-speech tagging. The underlying principle
  of this model is then applied to design a sequence-to-sequence
  inverse reinforcement learning framework that minimizes computational
  costs without compromising performance. The code for these models is
  available on the GitHub repository at
  https://github.com/shiizhI/FastTransformer.

model evaluation in 
  the field of deep learning, particularly in situations where multiple initial
  random parameters yield significantly different results.
  The study in question utilizes a straightforward multi-initialization ensemble
  method to examine whether multiple distinct models with similar performance 
  can be effective for real-world tasks.
  After determining suitable hyperparameters and selecting a robust training 
  regimen, researchers trained a ResNet-50 on ImageNet with 300 different 
  initial random parameters and assessed the resulting models in various ways.
  The main findings indicate that despite the large initial diversity, the 
  models showed only a mild increase in performance when trained with 30 times 
  more data, and the diversity did not appreciably impact performance on 
  subsequent tasks through feature transfer and multi-task learning. 
  However, the models exhibited notable difficulty generalizing outside their 
  training set, displaying a tendency to specialize in individual image 
  classes with little overlap, along with a significant decrease in their 
  functional ensemble performance when applied to real-world, diverse data 
  scenarios. 
  The research also uncovered that a significant subset of these models were 
  essentially distinct from one another, with no clear indication of why 
  this was the case, suggesting that deep learning's behavior under multiple 
  initial conditions remains an area in need of further exploration. 
  The study's results are made openly available, along with code and pre-trained 
  model weights, to facilitate replication and potential innovative uses. 
  Although the research did not uncover a compelling reason to adopt ensemble 
  methods in situations with diverse, high-performance models, it is essential 
  to note that such methods may still be valuable in situations where the 
  models' diversity is limited due to constraints such as budget caps on 
  training data, computational resources, or the number of initial random 
  parameters. 
  The research highlights the complexity of deep learning's initial conditions 
  and the need for further study, while also emphasizing the potential 
  benefits and simple implementation of ensemble methods in the field. 
  The study's findings also suggest that future work on the subject could 
  benefit from integrating theory and empirical evidence, as seen in the 
  nature versus nurture debate in psychology and biology. 
  The research on the 300 diverse ResNet-50 models is made openly available, 
  along with code, pre-trained model weights, and detailed documentation, 
  at https://github.com/vxx893/resnet-50-diversity.

molecular mechanics methods require a vast  
  amount of data, specifically bond, angle, and dihedral potential energy surfaces.
  These surfaces are not as comprehensively established as their corresponding  
  electronic properties, leading to limitations in accurately representing  
  polyatomic molecules and molecular interactions.
  Multi-configurational self-consistent field methods can simulate these  
  electronic properties in depth, offering a different approach to defining FF  
  potentials, which we refer to as ab initio FFs.
  By utilizing these detailed electronic structure models, ab initio FFs can  
  accurately capture complex molecular phenomena, such as multicovalency and  
  charge transfer, and significantly improve the representation of molecular  
  interactions, particularly for polar and aromatic bonds.
  This paper outlines the development of a new ab initio FF called BAC-FF,  
  specifically designed for polyatomic molecules, which incorporates a  
  multi-configuration complete active space self-consistent field method with  
  attachment block configuration tools to model attachment and detachment  
  processes, and includes a simple reorganization energy parameterization to  
  define potentials.
  The BAC-FF approach demonstrates improved results over traditional methods  
  in representing potential energy surfaces, especially for molecules with  
  multicovalent bonds, and reduces errors in first-order Nuclei-In-Motion  
  perturbation theory to a degree comparable to complete active space perturbation  
  theory.
  This method has been effective in accurately capturing complex molecular  
  phenomena and represents a reliable alternative for developing ab initio  
  force fields capable of simulating a wide range of molecular interactions. 
  The code is available at https://github.com/ChemTheoryLab/BACFF. 
  We also provide the trained parameters and testing datasets for other researchers 
  to use and compare with the BAC-FF method.

  van der Waals, and lone pairs. 
  The database contains over 30 million small molecular structures.

  where developers optimize program instructions to satisfy certain prerequisites, 
  with the aim of making verification more efficient. This technique has given rise 
  to a new category of tuned instructions that utilize additional bits to verify 
  preconditions before executing operations, thereby preventing undesirable effects 
  of certain operations on the program's memory. However, these tuned instructions 
  may lead to a decrease in overall performance, making it crucial to find a balanced 
  solution. This paper presents a novel approach called Typhon, which is an 
  instruction-tuning-based memory protection technique that focuses on verifiably 
  preventing the effects of floating-point operations that cause division-by-zero 
  errors on the program's memory. Additionally, Typhon differentiates itself from 
  existing solutions by incorporating a precise and efficient method for identifying 
  verifiable areas of floating-point code, in addition to providing a tuned 
  instruction that can detect division-by-zero errors at a lower performance cost. 
  The results of our research demonstrate that Typhon leads to a significant 
  performance improvement over existing solutions, with a 10 times lower overhead of 
  instruction execution and a 30 times lower overhead of page table updates. 
  Furthermore, Typhon's approach of distinguishing verifiable areas of floating-point 
  code through pattern matching allows it to handle complex patterns at a decent 
  speed, resulting in Typhon's ability to handle a majority of real-world RE2C 
  benchmarks with only a minimal loss in performance. 
  The Typhon instruction and verifier were implemented as part of the Venidia 
  verification framework and the Venidia compiler, respectively, with the Typhon 
  instruction being compatible with popular verification frameworks like Venidia, 
  VxWorks, and QEMU, and the Venidia compiler being compatible with Venidia and 
  VxWorks.

As freezing progresses, the droplet's evaporation behavior changes in response to the growing ice interface, ultimately leading to a localized deposit at the droplet's center when the ice layer becomes sufficiently thick. Our findings demonstrate that the salt residue's pattern can be wholly reproduced from a single frame of the freezing process, enabling the retrieval of valuable information about the freezing process from post-mortem analysis of the residue. By interpreting the residue patterns through the curve of their maximum curvature, we gain insight into the freezing process at various scales, from the microscopic to the mesoscopic. Our study shows that the information retained in the residue pattern can be utilized in a data-driven approach to forecast the freezing process that produced it, and demonstrates the potential of this approach in predicting complex freezing processes from an individual frame of the freezing process. Our study also highlights the potential of the salt residue as a proxy for the freezing process that occurred on an icy surface, offering a non-invasive and visually interpretable method for analyzing the freezing process that could be employed in a range of contexts, from the study of laboratory experiments to the examination of natural phenomena. assembly model seeks to establish a lower
  bound on the number of configuration sequences required to assemble a given
  shape using square tiles, with the constraint that each tile is placed in a
  two-dimensional space without knowledge of future placements. This problem has
  an equivalent in the 1D assembly model, where a chain of squares needs to be
  assembled from the left end, with the placement of each square determining
  the length of the chain and the allowed gap between adjacent squares being
  unknown at the time of placement. In this 1D version, the goal is to create
  a chain of a specified maximum length using a set of squares, with lengths
  ranging from 1 to n-1, where n represents the desired chain length.
  A significant result in this area demonstrates that in the 1D assembly model,
  there exists a lower bound on the length of chains that can be assembled,
  specifically n >= 2^log(n) - 1, with log denoting the logarithm to the
  base 2. This result implies that the 1D assembly model can simulate the
  Turing machine model, where the tape in the Turing machine model is
  equivalent to the chain in the 1D assembly model, with each square
  corresponding to a binary digit in the Turing machine model.
  This 1D assembly model has a corresponding diagonal assembly model, where the
  placement of squares is determined by the x and y coordinates of the
  assembly space. In this model, a square with coordinates (x1, y1) and (x2,
  y2) can be placed if |x1 - x2| <= |y1 - y2| or |x2 - x1| <= |y2 -
  y1|, with the goal of assembling a chain of a specified maximum length.
  A result in this area demonstrates that there exists a chain that requires
  n >= 2^log(n) - 1 squares to assemble in the diagonal assembly model.
  This result was discovered by Ruoxi Sun.  This result has a corresponding
  claim in the planar assembly model that was initially proved by David
  Mix Barrington, Shyam Sung, and Pierre Senellart, with an upper bound
  of n+1 squares, and was later narrowed to n squares by Ruoxi Sun.
  This result has a publication in the journal Theory of Computing Systems

  algorithms have been developed and are widely used due to their efficiency.
  However, there is a lack of systematic evaluation for these algorithms.
  To address this gap, we present a comprehensive framework for evaluating
  dense image matching algorithms.  This framework is designed to work with
  ground truth data obtained from multi-view stereo.  It includes metrics for
  assessing point cloud completeness and density, as well as relative pose
  accuracy.  We extracted and processed 30 dense matching algorithms from
  OpenCV, CMU's PCL, and the research literature.  These algorithms were
  tested using nine challenging sequences captured in real-world settings.
  The results showed that algorithms performing outlier rejection consistently
  produce better results than those that do not.  Furthermore, our study
  revealed that spatially-weighted Gaussian filters can significantly
  outperform conventional Gaussian filters before applying matching algorithms.
  Additionally, the location of the filter within the image processing
  pipeline was found to impact the result, with applying a filter at the
  beginning resulting in better results than applying it at the end.
  Notably, our evaluation framework demonstrated that training-based matching
  algorithms can produce results comparable to state-of-the-art sparse image
  matching algorithms in certain scenarios.  The code and data for this study
  are available online at https://github.com/PRM14/Dense_Image_Matching_Evaluation. 
  This repository also serves as a starting point for developing a unified
  dense image matching API. 
  We hope that our findings and the provided resources will contribute to
  further research and development in dense image matching. 
  To facilitate this process, we propose a set of guidelines for testing
  dense image matching algorithms in real-world settings. 
  These guidelines involve applying a pre-trained, non-local mean filter
  prior to running the matching algorithm, and incorporating spatially
  weighted averaging for aggregating matching results. 
  We also recommend incorporating a minimum curvature constraint in the
  evaluation process. 
  Finally, we believe that a unified dense image matching API is essential
  for advancing this technology and encourage the community to support
  this initiative.

In contrast, in the simulations with lower Coriolis forces, the zonal flows fluctuated constantly and failed to maintain their stability. Our analysis suggests that the breakdown of the zonal flow stream function in the lower-Coriolis simulations is linked to the failure of the shearing box to establish a stable, meridionally elongated circulation. As a result, the zonal flow's angular momentum transport reverses, leading to a further decline in its stability. Our study supports previous findings indicating that the zonal flow's stability is influenced by its own strength, but also reveals an additional factor at play - the strength of the Coriolis force. Our data shows that the zonal flow's diffusion rate increases with a decrease in the Coriolis force, occurring at a rate of 0.05-0.1 per rotation periods. Our research further reveals that the zonal flow's onset is delayed in simulations with both high and low Coriolis forces when we used a smaller initial random perturbation, suggesting that both a strong and a weak Coriolis force are necessary for the development of zonal flows. This approach, which we call the "alternating nested pushdown" (ANPD) method, serves as the foundation for an automated solving system for alternating nested QBFs (ANQBFs). The ANPQ solver leverages this strategy and employs a pushdown architecture to manage the nested universals, effectively treating each one as a new variable.

  The alternating nested pushdown approach yields an average solving time of approximately 2 seconds for the hard instances from the nest2005 benchmark set, outperforming other state-of-the-art solvers such as the 2016 QBF solving competition winner, the 2016 CADE competition winner, and the 2017 FLoP competition winner.

To better understand these dynamics, we analyzed a coronal hole observed during an equatorial passage of the Sun by the Interface to the Magnetic Solar Convective Boundary using a high-resolution, three-dimensional numerical model. By examining the relationship between subsonic winds in the convective boundary and the properties of the overlying corona, our simulation revealed that the wind accretion speeds are generally rapid in the upper photosphere and remain relatively constant at approximately 4.5 km s-1 throughout the convective boundary. As a result, our simulation suggests a limited range of values for the surface integral of the wind accretion, which could help explain the observed constancy of the radiative loss rate across coronal holes. Consequently, these findings imply that the driving force for coronal heating and solar wind formation might be relatively stable and resistant to changes in the solar cycle. Furthermore, our simulation showed that the distribution of X-ray and extreme ultraviolet emission is only marginally affected by the wind accretion, indicating that the atmospheric response to the convective boundary remains stable and resistant to changes in the solar cycle. Consequently, these findings suggest a simplified model in which the convective boundary is treated as a constant, random, and uniform noise source. As such, this model replicates the observed characteristics of the radiative loss rate and distribution of X-ray and extreme ultraviolet emission across coronal holes. Nevertheless, our simulation's limitations highlight the necessity for high-resolution, three-dimensional models that can accurately capture the random and inhomogeneous features of the convective boundary. Ultimately, these models are essential for a more comprehensive understanding of the dynamics governing coronal heating and solar wind formation.
